Bolzen.et: From Middle High German bolz, from Old High German bolz, from Proto-West Germanic *bolt. Compare Dutch bout, English bolt, Danish bolt, Icelandic bolti.

s: a gun or cannon used for salutes

s: a thickish, roundish object: bulb, tuber
Bolle.et: From Middle High German bolle, from Old High German bolla, from Proto-West Germanic *bollā, from Proto-Germanic *bullǭ.

s: female Bolivian, female person from Bolivia

Boltzmann-Konstante.et: From Boltzmann + Konstante (“constant”), from the surname of Ludwig Boltzmann.

Bollwerk.et: From Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bolwerk.

s: upper leg, thigh (including the buttock), especially when sturdy or fleshy, now most often said of slaughtered poultry
Bollen.et: Of dialectal origin, from Middle Low German bolle m or f, which is the same word as Bolle f (“roundish object”, etymology 2). The sense “thigh” probably developed under influence of (remotely related) Middle Low German bille, for which see Dutch bil (“buttock”…

Bollerwagen.et:
bollern (“to rumble, to bang, to thud”) + Wagen (“vehicle”). See also poltern.
Compare Dutch bolderwagen, bolderkar.

-bold.et: Related to bald, in the obsolete sense “daring”, compare English bold.

s: Die Berliner sind etwas bollerig, aber nicht die schlechtesten Menschen.
Berliners are rather loud and gruff, but not the worst of people.
bollerig.et: From bollern (“to thud, rumble”) + -ig. The former is a variant of poltern.

Bollchen.et: Borrowed from Low German Bolltje, diminutive of Boll (“roundish object”), from Proto-Germanic *bullǭ. Equivalent to Bolle (“bulb, tuber”) + -chen. Cognate with Dutch bolletje, Danish bolsje.

Böll.et:
From Middle Low German boll (“rounded hill”), from Old Saxon bollo, from Proto-Germanic *bullô (“round object”). Compare Boller.
Also from the old Germanic name Baldo, see Bold. Compare Boell.

s: Böllen (a village in southern Baden-Württemberg, Germany)
to light firecrackers or fireworks, especially loud ones
to make loud banging sounds (of salute cannons, etc.)
